What is boundary value analysis?.raw:
Boundary value analysis (BVA) is a black-box testing technique that designs test cases around the edges of the input domain. The reasoning behind it is that programmers most often make mistakes at the boundaries of a range — the minimum, the maximum, and the values immediately inside and outside them [1].

**How it works in practice**

- For a field accepting integers from 1 to 100 inclusive, BVA suggests testing 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101 [1].
- The classic three-point rule tests minimum, minimum minus one, minimum plus one, and maximum, maximum minus one, maximum plus one — six test cases in total [1].

**How it fits with equivalence partitioning**

BVA pairs naturally with equivalence partitioning. EP first divides the input domain into classes of values that should behave the same, and BVA then picks the values at the edges of each class, where off-by-one errors are most likely to hide [1]. EP itself draws classes from both valid and invalid inputs, and a complete test set samples at least one value from each class [2].

passages.text:
Equivalence partitioning, or EP, divides the input domain of a program into
equivalence classes: groups of values the program is expected to treat identically.
Testing one representative value from each class is assumed to reveal the same faults
as testing every member of the class, so EP greatly reduces the number of test cases.

Partitions are drawn from both valid and invalid inputs. For an age field that accepts
0 to 120, the valid class is the range 0 to 120, and there are two invalid classes:
negative values and values above 120. A complete test set samples at least one value
from each class.

When a program takes several inputs, EP considers each input's classes independently
and then combines representative values, usually with an all-combinations or pairwise
strategy. The resulting test suite is much smaller than exhaustive testing but still
covers every behaviourally distinct category of input.

passages.title: Statement and Branch Coverage
passages.heading: Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
passages.text:
Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
exercises. A suite reaches one hundred percent statement coverage when every line of
code has been run at least once. Statement coverage is the weakest structural coverage
criterion, because it can pass while the suite misses many bugs in decisions.

Branch coverage is stronger. It requires every decision in the program, such as an if
or a switch, to take both the true and the false outcome at least once. For an if
statement with no else clause, branch coverage still demands one test that skips the
body and one test that enters it.

Branch coverage is often called decision coverage. It subsumes statement coverage:
reaching full branch coverage also gives full statement coverage, because every
statement lies on some branch. A test suite that achieves branch coverage but not
condition coverage may still miss bugs that depend on the combination of several
conditions inside a single decision.

What is equivalence partitioning?.raw:
Equivalence partitioning (EP) is a testing technique that divides a program's input domain into equivalence classes — groups of values the program is expected to treat identically [1]. The idea is that testing one representative value from each class should reveal the same faults as testing every member, so EP greatly reduces the number of test cases you need [1].

Key points:

- Both valid and invalid inputs are partitioned. For an age field accepting 0 to 120, the valid class is the range 0 to 120, and there are two invalid classes: negative values and values above 120 [1].
- A complete test set samples at least one value from each class [1].
- When a program has several inputs, EP treats each input's classes independently and then combines representative values, usually with an all-combinations or pairwise strategy [1]. The resulting suite is much smaller than exhaustive testing but still covers every behaviourally distinct category of input [1].

EP also pairs naturally with boundary value analysis: EP divides the domain into classes, and BVA then picks the values at the edges of each class, where off-by-one errors are most likely to hide [2].

What is the difference between statement.raw:
**Statement coverage** measures the share of executable statements a test suite runs. A suite hits 100% statement coverage when every line of code has been executed at least once [1].

**Branch coverage** is stricter. It requires every decision (an if, a switch, etc.) to take both the true and the false outcome at least once. Even an if with no else clause needs one test that skips the body and one that enters it [1].

Key differences:

- Branch coverage is the stronger criterion; statement coverage is the weakest structural coverage criterion, because a suite can reach full statement coverage while still missing many bugs in decisions [1].
- Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage. Full branch coverage guarantees full statement coverage, since every statement lies on some branch [1].
- Branch coverage is also called decision coverage [1].
- Even branch coverage has limits: a suite that achieves branch coverage but not condition coverage may still miss bugs that depend on combinations of several conditions inside a single decision [1].

How do boundary value analysis and equiv.raw:
They are complementary techniques: equivalence partitioning (EP) decides **where the behaviour changes**, and boundary value analysis (BVA) then tests **the edges of those regions**, where off-by-one bugs are most likely [1].

- EP divides the input domain into equivalence classes that should behave the same, then samples one representative value from each class to reduce the number of tests [2].
- BVA focuses on the minimum, maximum, and values immediately inside and outside a range, because mistakes cluster at boundaries [1].
- BVA "pairs naturally" with EP: EP first forms the classes, and BVA picks values at the edges of each class [1].
- EP includes both valid and invalid classes, such as negative values and values above 120 for an age field accepting 0 to 120 [2]. Testing at the edges of those classes is exactly where BVA is useful [1].

For example, for a field accepting 1 to 100 inclusive, EP would identify the valid class and invalid classes, while BVA would test 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101 using the classic three-point rule [1].

summary:boundary-value-analysis.raw:
## Boundary Value Analysis (BVA)

- BVA is a black-box testing technique that designs test cases around the edges of the input domain [1].
- The underlying idea: programmers most often make mistakes at the boundaries of a range — the minimum, the maximum, and the values immediately inside and outside them [1].
- Worked example: for a field that accepts integers from 1 to 100 inclusive, BVA suggests testing 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101 [1].
- The classic three-point rule tests the minimum, minimum minus one and minimum plus one, plus the maximum, maximum minus one and maximum plus one, giving six test cases in total [1].

## Combining BVA with Equivalence Partitioning

- BVA pairs naturally with equivalence partitioning [1].
- Equivalence partitioning first divides the input domain into classes of values that should behave the same [1].
- Boundary value analysis then picks the values at the edges of each class, where off-by-one errors are most likely to hide [1].

passages.title: Statement and Branch Coverage
passages.heading: Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
passages.text:
Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
exercises. A suite reaches one hundred percent statement coverage when every line of
code has been run at least once. Statement coverage is the weakest structural coverage
criterion, because it can pass while the suite misses many bugs in decisions.

Branch coverage is stronger. It requires every decision in the program, such as an if
or a switch, to take both the true and the false outcome at least once. For an if
statement with no else clause, branch coverage still demands one test that skips the
body and one test that enters it.

reaching full branch coverage also gives full statement coverage, because every
statement lies on some branch. A test suite that achieves branch coverage but not
condition coverage may still miss bugs that depend on the combination of several
conditions inside a single decision.

study_guide:quantum entanglement (off-sy.raw:
## Quantum Entanglement

This isn't covered in your course materials, so here's a general explanation:

- Quantum entanglement is a phenomenon where two or more particles become linked so that their measurable properties are correlated, no matter how far apart they are.
- Entangled particles are described by a single shared quantum state rather than by independent states for each particle.
- Measuring one particle immediately constrains what will be measured on its partner; for example, if one of an entangled pair is measured with spin up, the other will be found spin down when measured along the same axis.
- This correlation does not allow faster-than-light communication: each individual measurement result still looks random, and the correlation only becomes visible when the two sets of results are compared through an ordinary, slower-than-light channel.
- The effect is commonly demonstrated with pairs of photons or electrons, and it is the basis of ideas such as quantum teleportation, quantum cryptography, and some approaches to quantum computing.
- Entanglement is fragile; interaction with the environment causes decoherence, which degrades the shared state, so experiments require careful isolation and error correction.

Note: your course passages cover software testing topics (boundary value analysis, equivalence partitioning, statement and branch coverage), which are unrelated to this topic.

Which six values does boundary value ana.raw:
For a field that accepts integers from 1 to 100 inclusive, BVA tests these six values [1]:

- 0 — minimum minus one
- 1 — the minimum
- 2 — minimum plus one
- 99 — maximum minus one
- 100 — the maximum
- 101 — maximum plus one

This comes from the classic three-point rule, which tests the minimum, minimum minus one and minimum plus one, plus the maximum, maximum minus one and maximum plus one, giving six test cases [1]. The reasoning is that off-by-one errors cluster at the edges of a range [1].

Statement coverage measures the share of executable statements that a test suite
exercises. A suite reaches one hundred percent statement coverage when every line of
code has been run at least once. Statement coverage is the weakest structural coverage
criterion, because it can pass while the suite misses many bugs in decisions.

Branch coverage is stronger. It requires every decision in the program, such as an if
or a switch, to take both the true and the false outcome at least once. For an if
statement with no else clause, branch coverage still demands one test that skips the
body and one test that enters it.

Branch coverage is often called decision coverage. It subsumes statement coverage:
reaching full branch coverage also gives full statement coverage, because every
statement lies on some branch. A test suite that achieves branch coverage but not
condition coverage may still miss bugs that depend on the combination of several
conditions inside a single decision.

passages.title: Boundary Value Analysis
passages.heading: Boundary value analysis, usually shortened to BVA, is a black-box testing technique
passages.text:
Boundary value analysis, usually shortened to BVA, is a black-box testing technique
that designs test cases around the edges of the input domain. The idea is that
programmers most often make mistakes at the boundaries of a range, such as the
minimum, the maximum, and the values immediately inside and outside them.

For a field that accepts integers from 1 to 100 inclusive, BVA suggests testing the
values 0, 1, 2, 99, 100 and 101. The classic three-point rule tests the minimum, the
minimum minus one and the minimum plus one, plus the maximum, the maximum minus one
and the maximum plus one, which yields six test cases.

BVA pairs naturally with equivalence partitioning. Equivalence partitioning first
divides the input domain into classes of values that should behave the same, and then
boundary value analysis picks the values at the edges of each class, where off-by-one
errors are most likely to hide.

passages.title: Equivalence Partitioning
passages.heading: Equivalence partitioning, or EP, divides the input domain of a program into
passages.text:
Equivalence partitioning, or EP, divides the input domain of a program into
equivalence classes: groups of values the program is expected to treat identically.
Testing one representative value from each class is assumed to reveal the same faults
as testing every member of the class, so EP greatly reduces the number of test cases.

Partitions are drawn from both valid and invalid inputs. For an age field that accepts
0 to 120, the valid class is the range 0 to 120, and there are two invalid classes:
negative values and values above 120. A complete test set samples at least one value
from each class.

When a program takes several inputs, EP considers each input's classes independently
and then combines representative values, usually with an all-combinations or pairwise
strategy. The resulting test suite is much smaller than exhaustive testing but still
covers every behaviourally distinct category of input.
